main_message: Steel has always been about who controls the route from raw materials to finished product. Carnegie did it by buying the supply chain, governments now do it with tariffs and a veto share, and Europe is adding a carbon charge on top.
why_hook: The 'half of the world's steel, then almost the same amount, but now only four percent' puzzle is intriguing. The wording is clumsy, though. 'Nearly as much' and 'about four percent' sound like a contradiction until you work it out. The weapon question is a good one.
what_connects_layers: The repeated line 'who controls the path?' ties them together. Carnegie bought the supply chain, governments now decide who can sell, and carbon pricing adds a toll. It is neat, but the carbon layer feels bolted on. A tariff protects local industry, while a carbon price is meant to cut emissions, and the script doesn't say they have different goals.
ending_comment: Yes. Output stayed flat while the share fell, and control of the 'path' has moved to other countries and to governments. The last line about the Edgar Thomson works is a nice touch. The ending says whether it's worth the cost can't be settled, which feels like a bit of a dodge.

boring_or_slow.why: Lots of tonnages and mileages for ore, coal and limestone. The point, that geography and logistics decide the price, takes a while to land.
A stack of dates, proclamations and percentages (25, 50, 72, 77, 80). I lost track of which was which.
Many large numbers at once: 2.4 billion, 745 million, 131 million, 18.3 million. Too many to hold onto.
The CBAM details (50-tonne threshold, certificates, euros per tonne, deductions, free allowances) are dense and read like a regulation.

confusing.quote: nearly as much — and that was about four percent
confusing.why: I had to think hard to get that 'as much' means as much tonnage, not as much share. It sounds contradictory.

confusing.quote: a country can import its phones and still function
confusing.why: The 'skeleton' idea is fine, but the jump to 'a country that can't make steel' isn't explained. The US does still make 82 million tonnes.

confusing.quote: electric arc furnaces, which can run largely on scrap
confusing.why: I don't know why this matters yet. It only pays off in segment 10, and the numbers come back without much explanation.

confusing.quote: China's steel exports alone were larger than everything the United States produced
confusing.why: 131 million against 82 million is stated flatly, but it's unclear whether that is a problem or just a comparison.

confusing.quote: worth about one hundred ninety euros per ton
confusing.why: The script says this isn't what importers pay, but never gives the real figure, so I don't know what the actual cost is.

confusing.quote: a hydrogen route needs large amounts of clean electricity
confusing.why: Why does this mean 'shaped by where its inputs are'? The link to Pittsburgh is too brief to follow.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: the steel is typically exported at low prices
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: Almost all the evidence points to Chinese oversupply and subsidies. There is little on why China built so much capacity, or on what the tariffs cost users of steel such as carmakers and builders.
Utilization rising from 72% to 77% is presented next to a vague 'mixed effects' line. The downsides get one sentence and the supporting argument gets paragraphs.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: at a cost that no price list shows
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: The Homestead strike is told with casualties, while the efficiency gains get a more neutral tone. Fair enough, but it is a clear editorial lean.

claims_you_doubt.quote: That isn't a secret formula. It's geography plus logistics.
claims_you_doubt.why: Sounds too tidy. Carnegie's success surely also involved technology, management and deals, not just location.

claims_you_doubt.quote: steel power was never only about tonnage
claims_you_doubt.why: A neat conclusion, but I'm not convinced the 'who controls the path' idea explains modern tariffs. The script itself leans on overcapacity and subsidies, which is a different story.

claims_you_doubt.quote: a carbon price at the border sorts steel by how it was made, not where
claims_you_doubt.why: But the script also says it only favours steel from places that use more scrap, like the US. That sounds like it could end up working as a tariff in practice.

claims_you_doubt.quote: Tariffs, quotas and a golden share all decide who gets to use it
claims_you_doubt.why: Stretches the 'path' metaphor. A golden share that blocks plant closures isn't really about who uses a supply route.

best_moment: 09. The 'golden share' check. It tests the popular claim that Washington owns U.S. Steel, explains what the share actually allows, and gives the Granite City example. It's concrete, and it admits the full agreement isn't public.
top3_fixes: Rewrite the opening so the puzzle is easy to grasp on one hearing, for example: 'America makes about as much steel as in 1950, yet its share of the world has gone from half to four percent. So why is steel treated like a weapon?'

Cut the number density in segments 7, 8 and 10. Keep two or three key figures per segment, put the rest on screen, and add a one-line plain-language takeaway after each batch, including what the CBAM really costs an importer.

Give the other side more space and clarify the carbon layer. Add the costs of steel tariffs to steel users and consumers, and say outright that tariffs aim to protect local industry while CBAM aims to cut emissions, so the 'same machine' claim is argued rather than assumed.
